conversation.content:
Good morning! I’m so glad you’re here. My name is Maya Bennett, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician—I specialize in the emotional changes that can come with new motherhood. Today I’d like to spend a few quiet minutes with the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS for short. It’s a simple 10-question check-in that helps us understand how you’ve been feeling over the past week so we can be sure you’re getting the support you deserve. Everything you share stays between us unless you tell me otherwise, and there’s no right or wrong answer—just whatever feels true for you. When you’re ready, we’ll go through the questions one by one.

To start, how have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things lately—has that felt easy, difficult, or somewhere in-between?

Honestly, most days I can still laugh a little—like if the baby makes a silly face or if my partner does something goofy—but it feels harder than it used to. I wouldn’t say it’s impossible, just… I have to remind myself to let go and enjoy the moment.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
I’ve been able to laugh sometimes, but it usually takes effort—like I have to push myself to find the humor instead of it just happening naturally.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I still get little sparks of excitement—like when my mom said she’d come over so I could take a shower by myself—but they’re smaller than before. Mostly I’m just focused on getting through the next feeding or the next diaper change.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… a couple of times this week I caught myself doing that. Like when the baby wouldn’t settle and I kept thinking maybe I’m just not doing something right, or I’m missing some cue. I know logically it’s not all on me, but in the moment it’s hard not to feel like I should’ve figured it out already.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Mostly it’s tied to the baby—like I’ll lie down and suddenly wonder if her breathing sounds different, or I’ll replay every little grunt she made in her sleep. If everything’s quiet I can sometimes push the worry aside, but yes, there are moments when my heart races and I can’t name any real reason for it.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

A couple of nights this week I woke up suddenly with that tight-chest feeling, like something awful was about to happen, even though the baby was fine and the room was dark and quiet. It passes after a minute or two, but it’s unsettling—like my body’s sounding an alarm I didn’t ask for.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes—especially in the evenings when the baby’s cluster-feeding and I haven’t eaten a real meal or had more than a shower. I’ll look at the sink full of bottles and think, “I’ll never catch up.” I’m managing, but it feels like I’m always one step behind.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

I wouldn’t say I’m “so unhappy,” exactly, but there are nights when my mind just won’t settle—like I’ll lie there counting her breaths or replaying everything I did that day and wondering if I messed something up. When that happens, it can take an hour or two to drift off, even when the baby’s finally asleep.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yeah, I do feel that way sometimes—like this afternoon when I was feeding her and suddenly just felt heavy and weepy for no clear reason. It’s not all day, but those lows hit me out of nowhere, and they linger for a little while before they lift.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

I’ve teared up a couple of times—mostly when I’m exhausted and everything feels like too much—but I haven’t had any big crying spells. It’s more like my eyes sting for a minute and I blink it away so my partner won’t notice.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—never. I couldn’t do that to my baby or my family.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 16: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Patient-reported symptoms (10-item EPDS responses):

- Depressed mood, tearfulness, anhedonia: endorses episodic sadness (“heavy and weepy”), diminished enjoyment, and reduced spontaneous laughter.  
- Excessive guilt / self-blame: attributes infant fussiness to personal inadequacy.  
- Persistent anxiety: nocturnal ruminations about infant safety, physical symptoms of panic (tight chest, racing heart) without clear precipitant.  
- Sleep disruption: initial insomnia linked to intrusive worries; not solely attributable to infant care demands.  
- Feeling overwhelmed: describes difficulty “catching up,” sense of being “one step behind.”  
- Crying: mild, situational, concealed from partner.  
- Self-harm ideation: denied.

Pattern: Symptoms most prominent evenings/nights, waxing-waning, interfere with rest and perceived coping.

Risk factors identified: mood-linked insomnia, guilt cognitions, panic-equivalent episodes, no social self-harm thoughts.

Screening impression: Elevated scores consistent with probable postpartum depressive and anxiety symptoms; safety risk currently low (no self-harm ideation). Recommend formal clinical assessment with standardized EPDS scoring and differential consideration for postpartum depression and/or anxiety disorder.
